title: How to Get Your Students' Silent Attention Anytime You Want
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that the ability to get silent, immediate attention on command is a core diagnostic of good classroom management, and he specifically rejects gimmicky attention-getters like response claps or '123 eyes on me,' arguing they signal a teacher would merely like attention rather than actually requiring it. His recommended cue is a plain, firm phrase -- 'Can I have your attention please' -- delivered as a command rather than a genuine question, communicating an assumption of student capability and maturity. The concrete three-step method is: teach the exact expectation (stopping and looking within two seconds of hearing the cue begin), practice it using a designed noisy simulation like students chanting nonsense phrases before the cue is given, and test it under real conditions with a paired discussion activity, repeating until execution is consistently perfect. He closes by tying the technique to a broader SCM principle that skills transfer across domains -- from attention to behavior to academic performance -- so demanding excellence in this one routine has ripple effects elsewhere.
points: Gimmicky attention-getters like response claps or '123 eyes on me' are rejected because they signal the teacher only wants attention, not requires it.
The recommended cue -- 'Can I have your attention please' -- is phrased as a question but delivered and enforced as a command.
The three-step teaching sequence (teach, practice with a noisy simulation, test under real conditions) is designed to make silent attention automatic within a couple of days.
Because skills transfer across domains in Linsin's framework, mastering this one routine has ripple effects on broader behavior and work habits.
quotes: To be an effective teacher, you must be able to get your students’ silent attention anytime you want.

You also shouldn’t use silly response claps, “123 eyes on me,” train whistles, and other cutesy novelties to get them quiet. They communicate to students that you’d really like to get their attention but don’t actually require it.
It says what you want and expect. And though it’s phrased as one, it’s not a question. It’s a command.
As soon as they hear me begin to say “Can I have . . .” they stop, turn, and look in perfect silence.
If you’re a regular reader of SCM, then you know that everything transfers to everything else—from behavior to work habits to academic performance.
They love a leader that sets the bar high, shows them exactly how to reach it, and then allows them to do it all on their own.
